evidence.quote:
I. Overview
The paper offers a valuable literature review on Text and Data Mining (TDM), mapping the
complex regulatory framework surrounding these processes and shedding light on what
constitutes lawful TDM. However, several areas require improvement for the paper to reach its full
potential. This report provides some comments and suggestions to strengthen the paper's
structure, argumentation, and use of sources.
II. Comments
1) Introduction
○

○

Structure improvement: The introduction could be better structured to present the study's
subject matter clearly. The first two paragraphs are not sufficiently clear, particularly in
introducing the concept of "big data." It would be beneficial to discuss the characteristic
elements of big data and differentiate between structured, unstructured, and semistructured data. This is crucial for readers to grasp the subject thoroughly. For reference,
see Jonathan Grossman and Ami Pedahzur, [Ref:1]
Clarification of concepts: The sentence ‘data “is the new oil and lifeblood of economic
development” and just as oil needs to be burnt for it to be useful, raw data must be
processed to realise its true potential’ is problematic and contested. This analogy
oversimplifies the complexities of data processing in the digital economy. See, e.g., Clemens
Mewald, ‘Why Data Is *Not* the New Oil and Data Marketplaces Have Failed Us’ (Medium,
13 July 2023) [external resource identifier omitted] David Moschella, ‘Data Isn’t the New Oil; That
Might Be a Good Thing’ (2023) [external resource identifier omitted]




2) Regulatory Framework
A broader perspective is needed: The paper should more comprehensively address the regulatory
challenges of TDM, particularly from a data protection standpoint. This includes not only the
technical challenges of big data processing but also the legal issues associated with scraping and
mining of publicly available data. Including opinions from public agencies and supervisory bodies
would offer a more holistic view of the regulatory landscape. These perspectives could be
instrumental in identifying the main challenges to individual rights and public interests.
3) Data Protection Issues
○

○

○

○

○

Insufficient coverage of GDPR issues: The paper does not sufficiently address the
complexities and challenges that data mining poses for data subjects. The paper relies on
some sources of questionable quality. It would benefit from a more careful selection of
references, particularly those recognised as authoritative in the field. I recommend citing
more reliable sources, especially when describing the fundamental elements of GDPR, such
as Christopher Kuner and others (eds), [Ref:2],A Commentary (New York, 2020; online edn,
Oxford Academic); Indra Spiecker genannt Döhmann and others (eds), General Data
Protection Regulation: Article-by-article Commentary (München, 2023; Beck).
Concept of "meaningful research": The paper should elaborate on the idea of "meaningful
research" and how data protection regulations address data processing for scientific,
research, or statistical purposes. This is a critical aspect that currently needs more depth.
Data Protection by Design and Default: When discussing the implementation of the
principle of data protection by design and default, it is important to reference guidelines
issued by supervisory authorities. For instance, the EDPB Guidelines 4/2019 on Article 25
Data Protection by Design and by Default [Ref 5]; Commission Nationale d’Informatique et
des Libertés (CNIL), GDPR guide for developers (2022); Agencia Española de Protección de
Datos (AEPD), A Guide to Privacy by Design (2019).
Data mining, profiling and inferences: The paper should more comprehensively address the
challenges and risks of data mining, especially concerning profiling and the processing of
inferred data. The relevance of purpose limitation and data minimisation principles needs
more emphasis. Key references include Bart Custers and others (eds), [Ref:3,4]
Missing legal aspects. Data scraping: The paper currently lacks a discussion on the legal
aspects of data scraping at scale and text mining of publicly available data, which are
increasingly relevant, especially for training AI models. It would be beneficial to incorporate
an analysis of the legal challenges posed by these practices, e.g., Benjamin Bremert, Legal
Aspects of Text Mining Publicly Available Data, Unabhängiges Landeszentrum für Datenschutz
(ULD), 2017; Zuzanna Gulczynska, ‘Scraping personal data from internet pages - a
comparative analysis of the Polish Bisnode decision and the US hiQ Labs v LinkedIn Corp
judgment’, European Law Review, vol. 45, no. 6, pp. 857–869, 2020; Catherine Altobelli and
others, ‘To Scrape or Not to Scrape? The Lawfulness of Social Media Crawling under the
GDPR’, in Jean Herveg (ed), Deep Driving into Data Protection: 1979-2019: Celebrating 40 Years
of Privacy and Data Protection at the CRIDS (Larcier, 2021); Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens,
Richtlijnen scraping door private organisaties en particulieren (2024)




4) TDM and fundamental rights
Effectively addressing bias and discrimination in data mining is critical to safeguarding
fundamental rights. Failure to do so can result in inequitable outcomes that disproportionately
harm marginalised groups, perpetuating existing social inequalities. See Bettina Berendt and
Sören Preibusch, ‘Toward Accountable Discrimination-Aware Data Mining: The Importance of
Keeping the Human in the Loop-and Under the Looking Glass’, Big Data. 2017 Jun;5(2):135-152;
Solon Barocas and Andrew Selbst, ‘Big Data's Disparate Impact’, 104 California Law Review 671
(2016); Solon Barocas, ‘Data Mining and the Discourse on Discrimination’, Conference on
Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (2014).
5) Several footnotes and cross-references need to be revised and improved for accuracy and
clarity.
References
1. Grossman J, Pedahzur A: Political Science and Big Data: Structured Data, Unstructured Data, and
How to Use Them. Political Science Quarterly. 2020; 135 (2): 225-257 Publisher Full Text
2. The EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). 2020. Publisher Full Text
3. Discrimination and Privacy in the Information Society /authors.
4. A Right to Reasonable Inferences: Re-Thinking Data Protection Law in the Age of Big Data and
AI/authors.
Is the topic of the review discussed comprehensively in the context of the current
literature?
Yes
Are all factual statements correct and adequately supported by citations?
Partly
Is the review written in accessible language?
Partly
Are the conclusions drawn appropriate in the context of the current research literature?
Partly

Thank you very much for your constructive and insightful comments. I have thoroughly
revised the paper in light of your feedback, and I believe these changes have significantly
strengthened the review. Below, I address each of your comments and explain the
adjustments made.
1. Introduction: Structure and Clarity
I have restructured the introduction to improve clarity. The concept of "big data" is now
introduced with a more thorough explanation of its characteristic elements, including a
clearer distinction between structured and unstructured data. I have also reconsidered the
analogy of data being “the new oil,” and, following your advice, I have removed such
statements.
1. Regulatory Framework: Broader Perspective
The section on the regulatory framework has been expanded to offer a broader and more
comprehensive discussion of the legal challenges associated with TDM, particularly from a
data protection standpoint. I have added references to opinions from public agencies and
supervisory bodies to provide a more holistic view of the regulatory landscape. Data
Protection Issues: More Depth and Careful Source Selection The data protection section
has been substantially reworked to include more authoritative and recognised sources, as
you recommended. Additionally, I have expanded on the concept of "meaningful research,"
elaborating on how data protection regulations address the processing of data for scientific,
research, or statistical purposes. I have also incorporated references to the EDPB Guidelines
4/2019 on Article 25 (Data Protection by Design and Default), as you suggested. Data
Mining, Profiling, and Inferences I have significantly expanded the discussion on the
challenges and risks of data mining, particularly regarding profiling and the processing of
inferred data. Legal Aspects of Data Scraping I have added a paragraph discussing the
legal aspects of data scraping citing the sources that you had recommended.
1. Fundamental Rights: Bias and Discrimination
I have reworked the section on fundamental rights to more thoroughly address
the critical issues of bias and discrimination in data mining.
2. Footnotes and Cross-References
I have revised the footnotes and cross-references to improve their accuracy
and clarity. This includes correcting any inconsistencies and ensuring that all
references are properly cited and linked to the relevant sections of the paper.
Once again, thank you for your detailed feedback. I am confident that the revisions made in
response to your comments have strengthened the paper both in terms of structure and
substantive content.
○
